# Animated Label

Text that rolls when it changes state: the outgoing label lifts out while the incoming one rises from below, and the box eases between the two widths. The prose sibling of Animated Number: Next to Done, Weak to Strong.

```tsx
const [state, setState] = React.useState("Draft")

<AnimatedLabel swapKey={state} className="text-5xl font-semibold">
  {state}
</AnimatedLabel>
```

## Installation

```bash
# One-time setup (tokens + lib helpers)
npx koalaui-cli@latest init

# Add this component (its dependencies come along)
npx koalaui-cli@latest add animated-label
```

Manual: run `npm install radix-ui tailwind-variants tailwind-merge`, then copy the source into `components/ui/animated-label/` and adjust the import paths to your project. Components pull `cn` from `lib/utils`, the `tv` wrapper from `lib/tv`, and (for multi-part components) `createContext` from `lib/create-context`.

## Usage

```tsx title="usage.tsx"
import { AnimatedLabel } from "@/components/ui/animated-label"

export function Example({ expanded }: { expanded: boolean }) {
  // `swapKey` is what says the label now means something else; children alone
  // are new elements on every render, so they can't tell a state change apart.
  return (
    <AnimatedLabel swapKey={expanded ? "less" : "more"}>
      {expanded ? "Show less" : "Show more"}
    </AnimatedLabel>
  )
}
```

## Inside a button

When the whole label swaps, don't reach for this: give `Button` a `swapKey` and it wraps its children for you. Reach for `AnimatedLabel` when only part of the button should roll, the case below. `swapKey` boxes every child into the swap, so an icon left inside it dissolves and re-appears rather than turning; a caret has to sit outside the roll to rotate. The label still carries the width change, so the button morphs and the caret rides along.

This is the shape used by `LoadMoreTrigger`, `CodeSnippet` and the Chat reasoning trigger. The caret takes `caret-turn`, the shared disclosure beat - see [Motion](https://www.koalaui.com/docs/foundations/motion.md).

```tsx
<Button variant="secondary" aria-expanded={expanded} onClick={toggle}>
  <AnimatedLabel swapKey={expanded ? "less" : "more"}>
    {expanded ? "Show less" : "Show more"}
  </AnimatedLabel>
  <CaretDown weight="bold" className={cn("caret-turn", expanded && "rotate-180")} />
</Button>
```

## Alignment

The box is briefly a different width than the label it holds (that's the morph), so the label needs to know which edge to hold on to. `align` defaults to `center`, which is right inside a button. Left-aligned copy wants `start`, or the text drifts sideways as the box eases.

```tsx
<AnimatedLabel swapKey={state} align="start" className="text-lg font-medium">
  {state}
</AnimatedLabel>
```

## How it works

Two layers: the current label in normal flow, so it alone sizes the box, and a snapshot of the outgoing one taken out of flow on top of it, so it can leave without widening anything. Both run the `label-swap-*` keyframes at `--duration-base`, with the opacity front-loaded against the travel (solid by 45%) the same way the number roll does it: the two labels sit on top of each other, so a long half-visible cross-fade would read as one smeared word. The snapshot is `aria-hidden` and dropped as soon as its roll ends, so the accessible name flips straight to the new label.

The width is the part CSS can't express on its own, so it's driven from a layout effect: pin the old label's width, hand over the new one, release back to `auto` once it lands. The start value is read off the snapshot rather than remembered, so it can't go stale, and interrupting a morph starts from the width that's on screen rather than the one it was heading for. The first paint never rolls, and under `prefers-reduced-motion` the label simply swaps.

## API reference

### AnimatedLabel

One inline `<span>` whose layers are managed for you. Forwards all native `<span>` props; `className` (merged last) styles the label as a whole, so put a per-label color on a span inside the children instead.

| Prop | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| swapKey* | React.Key | - | Identifies the label on screen. Change it in step with the children and the two roll past each other. |
| align | "start" \| "center" \| "end" | "center" | The edge the label holds while the box eases between widths. Left-aligned copy wants `start`. |
| children | React.ReactNode | - | The label currently on screen. |

## FAQ

### Why do I need swapKey - can't it see the children changed?

Children are new React elements on every render, so the component can't tell an actual state change from a re-render; animating on identity would roll the label constantly. swapKey is the signal that the label now means something different. Often the text itself is the natural key (swapKey={label}).

### When do I use this instead of Button's swapKey?

Use Button's swapKey when the whole label swaps - it wraps the children for you. Use AnimatedLabel directly when only part of the content should roll, like a label sitting beside an icon that rotates rather than swaps, or when the label isn't in a button at all (a status word, a strength verdict).

### The color changes with the label. Which one does the outgoing text keep?

Whichever you put on the layer rather than the container. A class on AnimatedLabel itself lives above both layers, so the departing label would repaint to the new color; wrap the children in a span carrying the color instead and each label keeps the one it was born with. That's how PasswordStrength keeps Weak leaving red while Fair arrives orange.

### Does the width really animate, or is the box just as wide as the longest label?

It animates. The box is only ever as wide as the label it's showing; on a swap a layout effect pins the outgoing label's measured width and transitions to the incoming one, then releases the box back to auto. So neither state pays for the other's width at rest.

### What happens under reduced motion?

The roll and the width morph are both off and the label swaps instantly. The animation classes are motion-safe, and the outgoing layer rests at opacity 0 so nothing lingers over the new label.
